questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Jacobian of a Three-Dimensional Transformation
questions.problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(u\,v\,w) \\ u+2w \\ uv\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(u\,v\,w),\,y(u,v,w)=u+2w,\,z(u,v,w)=uv.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\frac{1}{u} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =\frac{1}{w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =2 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =u & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{u} & \frac{1}{v} & \frac{1}{w} \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ v & u & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{w}(-1)^{1+3}|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ v & u\end{aligned}|+2(-1)^{2+3}|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{u} & \frac{1}{v} \\ v & u\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{w}(u-0)-2(1-1) \\  & =\frac{u}{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Jacobian of a Three-Dimensional Transformation
questions.problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2} \\ u+3w \\ -v\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={u}^{2}+{v}^{2},\,y(u,v,w)=u+3w,\,z(u,v,w)=-v.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =3 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-1, & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 2v & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)(-1)^{3+2}|\begin{aligned}2u & 0 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =6u-0 \\  & =6u.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Jacobian of a Three-Dimensional Transformation
questions.problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u{e}^{w} \\ w-u \\ w{e}^{u}-3v\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u{e}^{w},\,y(u,v,w)=w-u,\,z(u,v,w)=w{e}^{u}-3v.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{w} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =u{e}^{w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =1 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =w{e}^{u} & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-3, & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & ={e}^{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{w} & 0 & u{e}^{w} \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \\ w{e}^{u} & -3 & {e}^{u}\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-3)(-1)^{3+2}|\begin{aligned}{e}^{w} & u{e}^{w} \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =3({e}^{w}+u{e}^{w}) \\  & =3{e}^{w}(1+u).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Jacobian of a Three-Dimensional Transformation
questions.problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T$ that maps the $uvw$-space into the $xyz$-space by means of the equations

$$
x=u{v}^{2}+w,\,y={u}^{3}+v,\,z=uv.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={v}^{2} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2uv & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =1 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =3{u}^{2} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =u & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & 2uv & 1 \\ 3{u}^{2} & 1 & 0 \\ v & u & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(-1)^{1+3}|\begin{aligned}3{u}^{2} & 1 \\ v & u\end{aligned}| \\  & =3{u}^{3}-v.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Jacobian of a Three-Dimensional Transformation
questions.problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}4v \\ 3{u}^{2}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(vw) \\ vw\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=4v,\,y(u,v,w)=3{u}^{2}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(vw),\,z(u,v,w)=vw.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =4 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =6u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-2w\operatorname{sin}⁡(vw) & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =-2v\operatorname{sin}⁡(vw) \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =w, & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 & 0 \\ 6u & -2w\operatorname{sin}⁡(vw) & -2v\operatorname{sin}⁡(vw) \\ 0 & w & v\end{aligned}| \\  & =4(-1)^{1+2}|\begin{aligned}6u & -2v\operatorname{sin}⁡(vw) \\ 0 & v\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4(6uv-0) \\  & =-24uv.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Critical Points of a Transformation
questions.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+3w \\ v+2w \\ {v}^{2}-u\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u+3w,\,y(u,v,w)=v+2w,\,z(u,v,w)={v}^{2}-u.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =3 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =2 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =2v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2v & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2v & 0\end{aligned}|+3|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(0-4v)+3(0+1) \\  & =3-4v.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 3-4v & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $3-4v=0$ defines the plane $v=\frac{3}{4}.$

choices.value: The critical points lie on the planes $v=\pm w.$
The critical points lie on the $uw-$ plane.
The critical points lie on the parabolic cylinder $w=\frac{{v}^{2}}{2}.$
The critical points lie on the plane $v=u.$
The critical points lie on the plane $v=\frac{3}{4}.$

answer_fields.correct_value: The critical points lie on the plane $v=\frac{3}{4}.$

questions.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}-{w}^{2} \\ w{e}^{u} \\ u-v\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={u}^{2}-{w}^{2},\,y(u,v,w)=w{e}^{u},\,z(u,v,w)=u-v.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =-2w \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =w{e}^{u} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & ={e}^{u} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 0 & -2w \\ w{e}^{u} & 0 & {e}^{u} \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u|\begin{aligned}0 & {e}^{u} \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}|-2w|\begin{aligned}w{e}^{u} & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u(0+{e}^{u})-2w(-w{e}^{u}-0) \\  & =2u{e}^{u}+2{w}^{2}{e}^{u} \\  & =2{e}^{u}({w}^{2}+u).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 2{e}^{u}({w}^{2}+u) & =0 \\ {w}^{2}+u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation ${w}^{2}+u=0$ defines the parabolic cylinder $u=-{w}^{2}.$

choices.value: The critical points lie on the plane $u=2v.$
The critical points lie on the parabolic cylinder $u=2{w}^{2}.$
The critical points lie on the plane $u=w.$
The critical points lie on the parabolic cylinder $u=-{w}^{2}.$
The critical points lie on the $vw-$plane.

answer_fields.correct_value: The critical points lie on the parabolic cylinder $u=-{w}^{2}.$

questions.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u \\ v{e}^{w} \\ 2u+v+3w\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u,\,y(u,v,w)=v{e}^{w},\,z(u,v,w)=2u+v+3w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & ={e}^{w} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =v{e}^{w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =2 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{w} & v{e}^{w} \\ 2 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =1|\begin{aligned}{e}^{w} & v{e}^{w} \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(3{e}^{w}-v{e}^{w}) \\  & ={e}^{w}(3-v).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ {e}^{w}(3-v) & =0 \\ 3-v & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $3-v=0$ defines the plane $v=3.$

choices.value: The critical points lie on the $uw-$plane.
The critical points lie on the plane $v=3.$
The critical points lie on the $uv-$plane.
The critical points lie on the cylinder ${v}^{2}+{w}^{2}=0.$
The critical points lie on the sphere ${u}^{2}+{v}^{2}+{w}^{2}=3.$

answer_fields.correct_value: The critical points lie on the plane $v=3.$

questions.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{u} \\ {e}^{u+w} \\ uv+w\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={e}^{u},\,y(u,v,w)={e}^{u+w},\,z(u,v,w)=uv+w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & ={e}^{u+w} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & ={e}^{u+w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =u & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{u} & 0 & 0 \\ {e}^{u+w} & 0 & {e}^{u+w} \\ v & u & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u}|\begin{aligned}0 & {e}^{u+w} \\ u & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u}(0-u{e}^{u+w}) \\  & =-u{e}^{2u+w}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ -u{e}^{2u+w} & =0 \\ u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $u=0$ defines the plane $u=0,$ i.e., $vw$-plane.

The critical points lie on the plane $2u+v+w=0.$
The critical points lie on the parabolic cylinder $w=-2{v}^{2}.$
The critical points lie on the plane $w=-2u.$
The critical points lie on the parabolic cylinder $w={u}^{2}.$

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=uv,\,y(u,v,w)=u+v,\,z(u,v,w)=w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}v & u & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1|\begin{aligned}v & u \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =v-u.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ v-u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $v-u=0$ defines the plane $v=u..$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Jacobian of an Inverse Transformation
questions.problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}xy \\ yz \\ xz\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x,y,z>0.$*
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=xy,\,v(x,y,z)=yz,\,w(x,y,z)=xz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =z & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =y \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}y & x & 0 \\ 0 & z & y \\ z & 0 & x\end{aligned}| \\  & =y|\begin{aligned}z & y \\ 0 & x\end{aligned}|-x|\begin{aligned}0 & y \\ z & x\end{aligned}| \\  & =y(xz-0)-x(0-yz) \\  & =xyz+xyz \\  & =2xyz.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2xyz & =2\sqrt{(xyz)^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{xy(yz)(xz)} \\  & =2\sqrt{uvw}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{uvw}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =-3 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =2 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =3 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 3 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-1|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}|-3|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-1(0-6)-3(-1-0) \\  & =6+3 \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}

Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x} \\ \sqrt{y}+z \\ {y}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x\ne 0$ and $y>0.$*
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{x},\,y(x,y,z)=\sqrt{y}+z,\,z(x,y,z)={y}^{2}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2y & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 0 & 2y & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 2y & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}} & =(\frac{1}{x})^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{{y}^{2}} \\  & ={u}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{w} \\  & =2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$

$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=x,\,v(x,y,z)=z-y,\,w(x,y,z)=xy.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ y & x & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ x & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(0-x) \\  & =-x.\end{aligned}

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-x & =-u\end{aligned}

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-u)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}-3{u}^{2} & 0 & 1 \\ 2v & 2u & 0 \\ 2u & 1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3{u}^{2}|\begin{aligned}2u & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}2v & 2u \\ 2u & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3{u}^{2}(0-0)+1(2v-4{u}^{2}) \\  & =2(v-2{u}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} =0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 2(v-2{u}^{2}) & =0 \\ v-2{u}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $v-2u^2 = 0$ defines the parabolic cylinder $v=2u^2.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Jacobian of an Inverse Transformation
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the transformation $\mathbf{T}:(u,v,w) \to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}(x,y,z)\to(u(x,y,z), v(x,y,z), w(x,y,z))$ is given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14045024/assets/9e6d498215d04524e5eec7343a1463a80182f3050eaf9ad5e4766cf7f5f50f14.png)

Find the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x>0$, $y \ne 0.$*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14045024/assets/8a59f6bb056b614f0489a4fbfcba7c97ca6fed48d754863514a6e08db5767cf2.png)

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given $\mathbf T^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ using the relation

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} \right)^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z) = x^2, \qquad 
v(x,y,z) = xy, \qquad
w(x,y,z) = yz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2x & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2x & 0 & 0 \\ y & x & 0 \\ 0 & z & y\end{aligned}| \\  & =2x|\begin{aligned}x & 0 \\ z & y\end{aligned}| \\  & =2x(xy-0) \\  & =2{x}^{2}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}y & =2\cdot x\cdot (xy) \\  & =2\cdot \sqrt{u}\cdot v \\  & =2v\sqrt{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2v\sqrt{u}}.\end{aligned}
$$
